title: Kansas police chief used Flock license plate cameras 164 times to track ex-girlfriend

reading.body:
This is an insider misuse case rather than a model error. A police chief with legitimate access to a license-plate reader network ran searches against a person he knew, repeatedly, over roughly five months, and the system returned the location data he was after. The failure sits at the query layer, where an authorized user turns a tool built for police work to a private purpose, and no technical safeguard or human check intervened before the conduct ended with his resignation.

Catching this would have required someone comparing the lookups to authorized casework. A plate reader network logs who searched what, so the material for detection exists at the point of use, but detection depends on a person or a rule reviewing those logs against a legitimate purpose, or on a control that requires each search to be tied to a case. The facts given do not establish what auditing or purpose restriction was in place, or whether any was reviewed.

What is not established: the account rests on a certification order described by a single outlet, and the number of searches is not consistent across the material, with the headline reporting 164 and the order as summarized reporting 228. The order is reported to record an admission that jealousy influenced his conduct, and the reporting does not establish whether any criminal charge followed.

reports.title: Kansas police chief used Flock license plate cameras 164 times to track ex-girlfriend

summary: According to a Kansas certification order, Sedgwick, Kansas, Police Chief Lee Nygaard reportedly used Flock Safety license-plate readers 228 times from June to October 2023 to check the whereabouts of his ex-girlfriend and her new boyfriend. The order said he also followed them in a police vehicle and admitted that jealousy influenced his conduct. Nygaard resigned in October 2023 and later lost his police certification.
